subject: English
topic: Degrees of comparison II — mixed tiers
description: Positive, comparative, superlative degrees; conversions; common errors

questions.stem: Convert positive to comparative: 'No other boy in the class is as tall as John.' becomes:

options.option_text: John is taller than any other boy in the class.
John is the tallest boy in the class always.
John is more tall than any other boys here.
John is as tall as any boys in his class.

questions.explanation: POSITIVE → COMPARATIVE conversion: 'No other X is as ADJ as Y' = 'Y is ADJ-er (or more ADJ) than ANY OTHER X'. Note: 'taller than ANY OTHER boy' (not 'than any boy', because that would include John himself). SUPERLATIVE = 'Y is the ADJ-est (most ADJ) of all'. Three degrees express the SAME idea: positive (with 'no other... as ... as'); comparative (with 'than any other'); superlative (with 'most ... of all'). PYQ STAPLE — conversion among degrees is heavily tested.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Degrees of comparison II — mixed tiers

options.option_text: Better (irregular form)
Gooder (regular form, wrong)
Best (the superlative form)
More good (English error)

questions.explanation: GOOD → BETTER (comparative) → BEST (superlative). IRREGULAR. Other irregulars: BAD → WORSE → WORST; LITTLE → LESS → LEAST; MUCH/MANY → MORE → MOST; FAR → FARTHER/FURTHER → FARTHEST/FURTHEST (FARTHER for distance; FURTHER for non-physical, e.g., 'further inquiry'); LATE → LATER/LATTER → LATEST/LAST. INSIGHT — REGULAR rules: 1-syl adj → +er/+est (tall, taller, tallest); 2+ syl → more/most (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful); 2-syl ending in y → change y to i + er/est (happy → happier → happiest).

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Of the two girls, Mira is the most intelligent.'

options.option_text: Should be 'more intelligent' (only 2 → comparative)
No error, sentence is correct already
'Two' should be replaced by 'both' here
'Mira' should not be mentioned at all

questions.explanation: RULE: when comparing TWO things → COMPARATIVE; THREE OR MORE → SUPERLATIVE. 'OF THE TWO' = only 2 → use COMPARATIVE 'MORE intelligent', NOT 'most'. Correct: 'Of the two girls, Mira is the more intelligent'. WHEN EXACTLY 2 are compared, English requires comparative. Other 2-vs-3+ markers: 'between A and B' → comparative ('the better of the two'); 'among A, B, C, ...' → superlative ('the best among the three'). PYQ FAVOURITE error.

questions.stem: Choose: 'He is more wiser than his brother.' This sentence has:

options.option_text: Double comparative error ('more' + 'wiser')
No error, perfectly grammatical
'More' wrong; should be 'most' (option here)
'Wiser' wrong; should be 'wise'

questions.explanation: DOUBLE COMPARISON ERROR. WISE is a 1-syllable adjective → comparative is WISER (or 'more wise', not both). Correct: 'He is WISER than his brother' (not 'more wiser'). Same errors: 'more better', 'most fastest', 'more easier'. RULE: NEVER combine '-er' with 'more' or '-est' with 'most'. INSIGHT — common Indian-English ESL trap; native speakers also slip ('most unique' technically wrong since 'unique' = absolute / non-gradable). ABSOLUTE adjectives without comparatives: unique, perfect, complete, infinite, dead, pregnant, equal — though informally graded ('more dead' for emphasis).

questions.stem: Convert positive to superlative: 'Very few cities in India are as crowded as Mumbai.' becomes:

options.option_text: Mumbai is one of the most crowded cities in India.
Mumbai is more crowded than other Indian cities entirely.
Few cities are as crowded as Mumbai in India here also.
Mumbai is the only crowded city of India here also.

questions.explanation: POSITIVE 'VERY FEW X are as ADJ as Y' = SUPERLATIVE 'Y is one of the MOST ADJ X'. Here: 'one of the most crowded cities in India'. Note 'ONE OF THE' — preserves original meaning that there are A FEW (not just one) cities equally crowded. If 'No other city' was used (instead of 'very few'), conversion would be 'Mumbai is THE most crowded city' (singular superlative). Three degrees: positive ('very few... as crowded as Mumbai'); comparative ('Mumbai is more crowded than most'); superlative ('one of the most crowded'). KEY: VERY FEW → ONE OF THE MOST; NO OTHER → THE MOST.

questions.stem: Choose the correct: '___ this exam, the previous one was much harder.'

options.option_text: Compared to (compared with also acceptable)
Comparing with (a wrong preposition)
In compare with (a wrong phrase)
Compare to (incomplete phrase form)

questions.explanation: Standard English: COMPARED TO + thing (showing similarity); COMPARED WITH + thing (showing both similarity + difference). 'COMPARED TO' is more common in everyday usage; 'COMPARED WITH' more formal. EQUIVALENT: 'In comparison with/to'. WRONG: 'compare with' (incomplete; missing -ed); 'comparing to/with' (gerund needs subject). PYQ TRAP — 'compare with' is also acceptable in some contexts (e.g., active comparison: 'I compare him with...'); but 'compared to/with' is the participial phrase form for setting up contrast.
questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Degrees of comparison II — mixed tiers

options.option_text: I am (using 'I' as subject)
Me (object pronoun, informal)
Mine (possessive pronoun)
Myself (reflexive pronoun)

questions.explanation: FORMALLY: 'than' is a CONJUNCTION followed by a clause: 'He is older than I (am old).' Pronoun = subject case ('I'). INFORMAL English: 'than' often treated as preposition: 'than me' (object case). Both common in usage, but 'than I' more formal/correct in standard grammar; 'than me' colloquial + spreading. EXAM PYQ: usually expects formal 'than I' / 'than I am'. SAME RULE: 'as ___ as' (e.g., 'as tall as I'). Pronoun-after-than tests are classic SSC questions.

questions.stem: Adjectives such as 'senior', 'junior', 'superior', and 'inferior' always take ___ instead of 'than' when making comparisons.

options.option_text: from — indicating distance or rank separation
to — because they are derived from Latin comparatives
than — following the standard comparative rule
over — to show precedence or authority in rank

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'senior', 'junior', 'superior', 'inferior', and 'anterior' are Latin-derived comparatives that already embed the comparative sense, so they take 'to' (e.g., 'He is senior to me'). Option C is wrong because the standard 'than' rule does NOT apply to this special group — 'He is senior than me' is a frequent and easily penalised error.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences contains a grammatical error in the use of degrees of comparison?

options.option_text: She is the cleverest student in the entire batch
This road is more longer than the state highway
He runs faster than anyone else in the relay team
That documentary was better than what I had expected

questions.explanation: B is a double comparative error: 'more' and the '-er' suffix cannot both be used together. The correct form is simply 'longer'. Option A is valid ('cleverest' is the standard superlative of 'clever'). Options C and D use comparative forms correctly. The tempting distractor is D, where some candidates wrongly suspect 'better than what' as an error — it is perfectly standard.

questions.stem: The superlative sentence 'Sachin Tendulkar is the greatest batsman of his era' correctly converts to the POSITIVE degree as:

options.option_text: Sachin Tendulkar is greater than every batsman of his era
No other batsman of his era is as great as Sachin Tendulkar
Sachin Tendulkar is great beyond every batsman in his era
All batsmen of his era are less great than Sachin Tendulkar

questions.explanation: The standard rule for superlative → positive conversion is: 'No other [noun] is as [adj] as [subject].' Option B follows this 'as…as' structure correctly. Option A is the comparative form ('greater than'), not positive. Option D uses 'less great than', which is also comparative. Option C is grammatically awkward and does not represent any recognised degree-of-comparison form.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence in which 'elder' is used INCORRECTLY according to standard English grammar.

options.option_text: My elder brother secured first rank in the university
She is elder than her colleague by nearly five years
The elder of the two brothers manages the family business
His elder daughter received the national bravery award

questions.explanation: 'Elder' can never be followed by 'than'; that construction belongs exclusively to 'older'. The correct sentence is 'She is older than her colleague by nearly five years.' Additionally, 'elder' is conventionally used only for family relationships, not for colleagues. Options A, C, and D all use 'elder' correctly in attributive position for family members.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the double comparative structure to express a proportional relationship?

options.option_text: The harder you study, more marks you will score in tests
The harder you study, the more marks you will score
Harder you study, the more marks you score in these tests
The harder you study, the more better marks you will score

questions.explanation: The double comparative structure demands 'the + comparative … the + comparative' in both clauses. Option B follows this exactly. Option A omits 'the' before the second comparative. Option C omits 'The' before the first comparative. Option D commits a double comparative error: 'better' is already the comparative of 'good', so prefixing 'more' is redundant and incorrect.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence that incorrectly uses a degree of comparison with an absolute adjective.

options.option_text: The city's infrastructure is more perfect than before the renovation
This is one of the most challenging exams in the country
The northern route is far less direct than the coastal highway
She is among the most experienced officers in the department

questions.explanation: 'Perfect' is an absolute adjective — it denotes a state that logically cannot admit degrees (something is either perfect or it is not), making 'more perfect' grammatically incorrect. Options B, C, and D are all valid: 'challenging', 'direct', and 'experienced' are gradable adjectives that legitimately take comparative and superlative forms. Candidates often accept A because 'more perfect' sounds natural in speech.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence that contains an illogical or incomplete comparison.

options.option_text: The climate of Ooty is far more pleasant than that of Chennai
The salary of a doctor is higher than an engineer in this firm
The wingspan of an eagle is much larger than that of a sparrow
Her writing style is more elaborate than that of her contemporaries

questions.explanation: Option B illogically compares 'the salary of a doctor' with 'an engineer' (a person), not with the engineer's salary. The correct form requires 'that of an engineer'. Options A, C, and D all use 'that of' to ensure parallel comparison — climate with climate, wingspan with wingspan, and writing style with writing style — demonstrating the correct technique this question tests.
